question: Integers \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c\) satisfy \(ab+c=100,\) \(bc+a=87,\) and \(ca+b=60.\) What is \(ab+bc+ca?\)
solution:
The first two right-hand sides differ by the prime number \(13\). Subtracting their equations produces a useful factorization:
\[
\begin{aligned}
13&=(ab+c)-(bc+a)\\
&=b(a-c)-(a-c)\\
&=(b-1)(a-c).
\end{aligned}
\]
Both factors are integers. Therefore \(b-1\) must be one of \(-1,1,13,-13\), giving exactly four cases.

- If \(b=0\), the first two equations give \(c=100\) and \(a=87\). But the third equation would require \(ac=60\), whereas \(ac=8700\).
- If \(b=2\), then \(a-c=13\) and \(ac=58\). The positive factor pairs of \(58\) are \((1,58)\) and \((2,29)\), with differences \(57\) and \(27\). Allowing both factors to be negative gives the same possible absolute differences, so \(a-c=13\) is impossible.
- If \(b=14\), then \(a-c=1\) and \(ac=46\). The positive factor pairs \((1,46)\) and \((2,23)\) have differences \(45\) and \(21\). Again, neither positive nor negative factors can have the required difference.
- If \(b=-12\), then \(a-c=-1\), so \(c=a+1\). Substitution into \(ab+c=100\) gives
\[
-12a+(a+1)=100,
\qquad -11a=99,
\qquad a=-9.
\]
Thus \(c=-8\). The remaining equations check:
\[
bc+a=96-9=87,
\qquad ca+b=72-12=60.
\]
This is the only surviving integer solution. Hence
\[
ab+bc+ca=108+96+72=\boxed{276},
\]
choice \(\text{D}\).
